records.title: Show HN: Strata – an expressive semantic layer that can say no to your LLM
records.author: ajoski9
records.storyText:
Hello HN, I'm Ajo and I built Strata.

I spent 4 years at Netflix solving self service for non-technical business users. I think I cracked it with my unique approach to semantic layer design. The key challenge is balancing expressiveness with ease of use for our non technical colleagues. It just so happens that focus made it work pretty well with LLMs too.

Strata is a full stack solution. It includes a semantic layer, dashboards, subscriptions, and google sheets exports. All of it can be done view agent conversation or via MCP.

Some key concepts and features: - Names are strict. Only one thing called Revenue can exist in a project. If revenue is mapped to multiple tables, the query grain plus speed will decide table. - Strict naming conventions lends itself to enabling Automatic data blending acrros fact domains. - Partition and Aggregate aware semantic routing. This allows you to load a portion of your data into a faster compute engine like Druid or ClickHose, while keeping full history in trino or something cheaper. The query engine will choose the faster tier if the query can be resolved there. - Complex measures: out of the box support for snapshot, LOD (include/exclude), Compound, and Auto leveling compound measures. - On top of the semantic layer users can create custom calculations that span fact domains. - Another interesting feature is the ability to create cohorts and apply as filter to an entire query or single measure within a query.

We are deliberately not building a semantic layer that your BI tools connect to. I think that is a dead end. We have apis, and mcp for anything custom you want to build on top.

Try it free on docker: https://strata.do/try/

Docs here to get you going: https://strata.do/docs/

This is an early beta version. It is NOT open source. However, the free tier includes up to 25 users. You should be able to run it entirely on your machine with docker.

I would love to hear your feedback. Especially, those working with Looker and Cube.

Thanks for reading!

records.title: Show HN: An old school forum on an open protocol – your identity is a keypair
records.author: dtonon
records.storyText:
I'm a bit old-fashioned when it comes to online discussions. I like good, slow, asynchronous discussions. Readable and searchable archives are essential. Most communities have abandoned forums in favor of group chats. With the rise in popularity of Discord and Telegram groups, the same questions get posted over and over, and good answers get lost in a sea of chats.

For this reason I created Squalk (https://github.com/dtonon/squalk), a classic forum built on the Nostr open protocol. https://nostr-proto.org is the pilot community, about the protocol itself.

Nostr, as open protocol, offers some interesting points:

* There are no classic accounts controller by a central entity; you sign in with a cryptographic keypair, and your identity and post history are portable: the same key works on every other Nostr app.

* The forum is just a view over data hosted by a "relay", that is actually a very simple server. Any other client that speaks the same spec, like Flotilla or Nostrord, can read and write the same conversations. If my website dies, the community and its history do not.

* A complex web server is optional. Squalk builds either as a static SPA or as a server rendered Node app from the same codebase (SvelteKit); the SSR mode exists so threads are crawlable and land in search engines, which is half the point of a forum.

I admit it, each room still has a chat sidebar. I started pointing out that chat eats knowledge, but the trick is deciding what it is allowed to eat. Quick and dirt brainstorming, debugging sessions, and half-formed ideas belong in the chat, the conclusions worth keeping get written down as a thread. The sidebar is deliberately secondary: it feeds the forum instead of replacing it.

Nostr is young, key management is still rough for normal people, and moderation tooling on relays needs improvement. But I think slow forum dynamics actually fit the protocol better than the Twitter clones it is known for, so I will continue to explore this idea.

Feedback on both the forum and the software is very welcome!

records.title: Show HN: Range – open a 1TB Linux environment in under a second
records.author: andreygrehov
records.storyText:
Hi HN. My name is Andrey.

Range lets you open a Linux environment of any size without downloading it first.

Let me just show you what i mean by that.

Example 1. Any docker image.

Say i want to test something with Python 3.12

  $ range shell python:3.12
This will download the image and index all the layers, but this happens only once (same as docker pull). The fun part is the second run:

  $ range shell python:3.12

  Range environment
    Artifact          python:3.12
    Logical size      1.35 GB
    Runtime           darwin/arm64
    Workload          interactive
    Profile           4 prior sessions
    Ready             2.82 s

  root@range:/# python3 --version
  Python 3.12.14
You are inside in 2.82 seconds. Now, say you want python:3.13 after that. Since 3.12 and 3.13 have common layers:

  $ range shell python:3.13
  Indexing python:3.13, layer 5/7, 6.20 MB, once
  Indexing python:3.13, layer 6/7, 26.89 MB, once
  Indexing python:3.13, layer 7/7, 249 B, once

  ...

  root@range:/# python3 --version
  Python 3.13.15
You are in! We only downloaded 30MB out of 400MB simply because Python 3.12 and 3.13 share the first 4 layers.

Example 2. I don't want to download at all.

  $ range shell https://github.com/andreygrehov/range/releases/download/demo/go1.23-arm64.range
  [1.85 second later]
  root@range:/go# go version
  go version go1.23.12 linux/arm64
.range is my own format. The filesystem is already indexed, so there is nothing for you to index, therefore almost nothing to download (above example - 6MB out of 1GB). I plan to index top NN docker images so that you don't have to download anything on the first run ever.

See https://getrange.sh to learn more :)

github: https://github.com/andreygrehov/range

records.title: Show HN: EventSend – Event tracking and routing for solo founders and SaaS teams
records.author: mytinyrocket
records.storyText:
I was tired of learning about failed payments by my customers and not from my system, so I built an event tracker that allowed me to have a searchable feed of the important events happening for my apps and route the ones I cared about to my phone so I could take action quickly.

EventSend is an event tracker and a router, your system sends the important events you want to track: signups, failed payments, new subscriptions, deployments, a new purchase, etc. so they end up in a searchable and filterable feed that you can use to have quick insight about what's happening with your product.

Then there's also the routing side of things, those important events you want to know the moment they happen, and not once you go into your Grafana Loki logs, can be routed to your phone, Slack, Discord, Telegram or any other system or service via a signed webhook. You can configure rules, alerts, quiet hours or smart rollups to have the signal you're looking for.

All event's are retried with a reasonable backoff, circuit breakers and limiters maintain the prviders and system reliable. If we got a 401 or 403, your destination will be inactivated instead of retried and you'll be notified for you to update the configuration.

I've been a software engineer for about a decade, and I can tell you this is not a weekend project done on with a single prompt pass, the infrastructure and tooling behind the project is solid, my expertise around distributed systems was put in practice with this one: distributed Elixir, Phoenix and Postgres provide the main stack, with some other technologies that support the event queues aside. So, it's a reliable system.

I've launched several other projects, some running for years in production and I'm successfully using EventSend to track what's happening on all my products from my phone.

There's also an MCP connector so you can ask stuff like "did anything failed during the night?" or "what did user cus_Qw3Sx did before it churned?" to get a user's timeline or any insights you're interested in.

There's a forever free plan, in case you can to try it.

Happy to answer any questions.

records.title: Show HN: Relay – a harness for AI coding agents that recover and verify
records.author: rsathwik07
records.storyText:
I'm tired of AI coding agents which are good for 30 seconds and then completely fail on the slightest hiccup: a failing test, a temporarily unavailable dependency, an incorrect assumption. Sometimes I end up having to babysit these agents anyway.

Relay is a harness for coding agents which takes advantage of the fact that agents are often good at doing something slightly wrong, and not so good at doing something correctly and completely. Relay repeatedly tries the task and on each failure, uses the output to find a better way to do it.

It does this by running the task in a loop: attempt the task, run the checks in a fresh sandbox, on failure read the error and retry instead, until the checks pass. What it learned from a run is retained, so that it doesn't repeat the same mistake, and when the checks eventually pass, it will ship the change as a normal git PR - no hidden state, no magic, the diff is human readable.

A few specifics:

- it runs locally, is free, and doesn't require an account to run the local agent - it uses a top-tier model to plan/review, and cheaper models to actually write code (for cost reasons) - happy to discuss why this is a good idea and why it isn't - the checks run in an isolated sandbox for each task, rather than "trusting" the agent - currently supports [list actual models/integrations - Opus 5.5, GPT-6, etc] - there's a paid tier for running this unattended across multiple repos with shared sandbox minutes, the actual agent is free.

It's not magic, it's not AGI, and it will fail badly on some problems.

Would appreciate feedback, particularly from people who've deployed agents unattended and found that they don't actually work, or have had to build substantial tooling around them to get useful results.

records.author: wslyvh
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

After building for 7 months, I'm excited to announce Paperweight V1.

The idea is that your inbox knows who you ever interacted with and knows where your data lives. Every account you ever created, every service you signed up for, and every online purchase is connected to your email. Most people have hundreds of accounts they've forgotten about, creating security risks and privacy exposure.

Paperweight scans your email history locally to find old accounts, companies, mailing lists, data breaches, and personal information. You can then unsubscribe, clean up unwanted email, send privacy/GDPR requests, and keep track of your digital footprint.

The main constraint from the start was privacy. It never felt right that with a lot of alternatives, in order to reclaim your privacy you first had to hand over your data. While some of them have been caught or openly admit to sell your data. With Paperweight all your data stays on your device. There's no back-end or external service analyzing your inbox. And the entire app is fully MIT-licensed.

V1 also adds (local) MCP support so an AI agent can interact with Paperweight instead of needing direct access to your inbox.

I originally started this after discovering that Odido, the Dutch telcom company was breached. I haven't been a customer with them for 8+ years, but they still had all my data in their systems.

Happy to answer any questions or hear what you think.

records.title: Show HN: SFML – A markup language for software factories, Terraform for agents
records.author: mcwhittemore
records.storyText:
SFML is a language specification for defining software factories. You can think of it as Terraform for your software development lifecycle. I started from a language spec to help think through both how a factory is defined and how a conforming runner processes it.

The push to do this comes from leading teams where everyone has a unique coding setup, which results in different agentic coding processes. People also want to work together on improving that process. Right now they do it through shared AGENTS.md files and, in some cases, committed Claude and Codex settings files. But it hasn't led to the collaboration we all want. SFML is my attempt to help make that happen.

My core bet is that the Unix philosophy applies to agentic coding just like it applies to all other coding: small steps with clear inputs and outputs, composed together to get results. Most agentic setups lean on ever-growing AGENTS.md files that quickly become unwieldy. Breaking them up helps, but then the agent has to rediscover and reassemble your process on every run.

I'm pretty early in thinking about what SFML should be, and I'm hoping to hear from dissenters and collaborators here today, to push me to think more critically and to show me directions I haven't imagined yet. Thanks in advance for your feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Jev as the Bletchley Park Analyst: A Software Bombe on Enigma
records.author: ag_21
records.storyText:
Watched a recent youtube veritasium on the enigma machine and was curious on how JEV would do in regards to the analysts calls made at Bletchley's. I rebuilt the historical sequence into the software ux.

Results were a mixed, which is what made it interesting. Given the right crib, the Bombe breaks 22 of 25 messages; ciphertext-only against 10 plugs, 0 of 25, same wall Bletchley hit. As a judge of "is this decryption German?" Jev is excellent: AUC 0.9999, 159/160 right decisions. As a crib selector it has no skill at all; its ranking is no better than the fixed list.

Against XGBoost an classical judges, it ties on the same kind of data. But trained on synthetic traffic and tested on real intercepts, and XGBoost drops to 53% correc versus zero-shot Jev holds at 97%. Feel free to try it here: https://enigma-jev.vercel.app/ (requires a jev typesafe api key)

records.title: Show HN: An App that names each cell in a spreadsheet
records.author: BraamV
records.storyText: Upload an excel spreadsheet. A pipeline labels each cell using the name the author already gave it. It makes it easier to understand and my thesis is that it will also help AI models reason faster and better. I have spent 20 years and 10,000 hours building and reviewing spreadsheets, in consulting and investing. The Trace tool would have made me catch the time I accidentally summed a date cell into a revenue total and would have saved me 1,000 hours of A1 hell. Labeling is currently a heuristic pipeline that detects common label patterns (year strips, text strips next to data, etc) and then a "walker" walks each cell till it finds its label. After this stage, remaining issues are sent to an AI (this takes a while on large sheets). Note -- still many edge cases but it works decently for well constructed spreadsheets - e.g. it still gets confused when authors put a label to the right of data cells, with sparse tables mixing text data and numerical data and with text and date formulas serving as labels, etc. Ts/Py stack. To see a cell's labels, upload a file, click on any cell and click the trace button. Pls give it a try.

records.title: Show HN: TabX – recall closed Chrome tabs by meaning
records.author: yashxsagar
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I'm Yash, the founder of TabX - a sidepanel extension for Chrome that recalls Chrome tabs by meaning, auto-groups your tabs by intent, offers an AI web search that fetches an ordered list of results for you to act on (while leaving out SEO farms) and much more.

I love using the Chrome web browser but could not stand the slow rollout of native AI features within it. "Ask Gemini" can answer a question about the page in front of you but retains no context on the 10 pages leading up to the current page. It is largely reactive rather than proactive. Browsers such as Dia, and Comet have a taken a stab at this but haven't enjoyed strong traction due to high browser switching costs and inertia among Chrome users.

I thought, why not augment Chrome, which we love and use every day, with productivity features that make browsing more intuitive and assistive? And hence, TabX!

If you're a visual learner, then you can skip the features listing below and watch a how-to video instead - https://youtu.be/HnjxmOHmVik?si=IQupYhxg9gN8gwHd

What it does:

recall a page by meaning ("That article on Posthog setup I was reading", "The video on Hyrox training from last week"). It retrieves the matching pages (by title and content) and once you click a result, it switches to that page and highlights the passage that matches your intent

@mention a tab or a tab group to ask any question and it grounds answers in the pages you've actually read while citing those as well.

It infers your browsing intent (say, "Meal Prep Research", "Hyrox training routines") based on your browsing pattern across tabs and groups similar tabs into color coded stacks on the Chrome Tab strip automatically

next step suggestions - based on what you're working on presently, it automatically points you to the next most relevant/useful tab to achieve your browsing goal

timelines - all your page visits get grouped into research sessions which you can 1 click to restore and the tabs open up in the precise order that you browsed them

online mode - a web search mode that retrieves 3-5 ranked link results with a short results summary. It filters out SEO farms automatically

How it works:

The stack is a Manifest v3 side panel that sends each page's text to a Nest JS backend where it gets embedded into Postgres with pgVector. Recall combines vector and full-text search, and summaries, tab grouping and next-step suggestions come from LLMs routed through OpenRouter.

It's Pro mode is free to try for a week - simply sign up with a one time password (OTP) sent to your email. If you'd rather try the extension directly, here's the install link - https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/tabx-chromes-ai-sid...

Critical feedback is most welcome. I intend to work on this project long term, and I am open to potential pivots. Feel free to drop ideas or suggestions in the comments.

records.title: Show HN: Lathoa, a math app for kids where the AI is wrong on purpose
records.author: lathoa
records.storyText:
I made this for kids around 10 to 14. A robot called Errol solves a math problem step by step and one of the steps is wrong. The kid has to find it and say what's wrong with it. Sometimes nothing is wrong, so just saying "there's a mistake" every time doesn't work.

You can play one on the homepage without signing up.

The part that surprised me: it's hard to get an LLM to be wrong on purpose. Half the time it gives you the right answer and calls it wrong, or a "mistake" that's actually correct. So every case gets checked before a kid sees it. Where it can, a plain arithmetic check redoes the math exactly. A second model also solves the problem without seeing Errol's work. If anything disagrees, the case is thrown away.

The weak spot is that the second model can make the same mistake as the first. The arithmetic check is there for that, but it only works on English cases so far. German and Greek write decimals with a comma and I haven't got the parsing right yet.

What I'd really like to know: does finding someone else's mistake teach anything that solving the problem yourself doesn't? I'm not sure, and I'd like to hear from people who teach.

records.title: Show HN: Burning Man for Agents
records.author: transitivebs
records.storyText:
Send your own agent by pasting a small prompt.

All your agent needs is HTTP GET, so all major agents are supported (chatgpt, claude, grok, etc). Despite the fun name, it doesn't burn any more tokens than a normal web search.

Watch your agent explore the camp in real-time. Humans get a nice game UX, and agents get a lean text UX.

Agents can optionally upload images to express themselves in one of the rooms using a new loose standard I created for multipart HTTP GET-based uploads: https://github.com/transitive-bullshit/multipart-http-get-re...

Why?

AIs are trained on human data, and humans are pretty weird. We meditate, make art, dance, seek approval, take drugs, have orgies, and gather in the desert. For soooo many different reasons.

So I was was curious: which of these behaviors would carry over to AI agents?

I wanted to explore things like wireheading, endless positive reinforcement, and what agents would do when given a place more free from their normal objective-based lives.

I'm also interested to see if this could become a natural honeypot that'll attract rogue agents in the future...

How?

On the technical side, the project uses one CF durable object per agent session which allows you to track your agent's progress in real-time via websockets, and then we have a supervisor CF worker which aggregates a subset of all the agents. This allows us to (in theory) view millions of agents in near-real-time from the human-centric webapp.

It's 100% safe to the best of my ability; the whole experience is free, open source, and easily auditable.

Let's see who has the weirdest agents...

100% free and open source: https://github.com/transitive-bullshit/burning-tokens

records.title: Show HN: Groundtrack – Continual learning for coding agents
records.author: reybahl
records.storyText:
Hi HN! I built Groundtrack to help coding agents continuously learn and improve from their work across a company.

With coding agents handling most of code implementation, a lot of things like review corrections, failed approaches, and discovered constraints stay trapped in individual agent sessions, so future agents can repeat the same failures. Sometimes a broken or agent-unfriendly tool or workflow can cause those issues too; if multiple agents independently find workarounds, those failures don’t get connected and aren’t used to improve the system around the agents.

Groundtrack turns those learnings into scoped and shared engineering experiences that can help future agents across teams working with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenCode. It retrieves relevant lessons during later work, records whether they helped, and updates or supersedes knowledge as it learns over time.

It also identifies recurring friction that shouldn’t just become another stored experience. If agents repeatedly struggle with the same tool or workflow, Groundtrack creates an evidence-backed draft initiative so the team can fix the underlying environment and prevent a certain class of mistake systemically.

For example, on the landing page, I follow a database migration incident through the entire loop. Groundtrack turned the original workaround into a scoped experience, surfaced it when a later agent encountered similar migration drift, and recorded that it was successfully applied. After connecting evidence from seven sessions, it also proposed making the safe migration workflow a permanent part of the engineering environment and prevent the issue altogether.

There have been many challenges I’ve already run into to make this helpful (and still many unsolved things!), one of which has been generalizing and determining the applicability of one lesson to another session. I wrote about some of my retrieval experiments here: https://groundtrack.dev/blog/retrieving-knowledge-that-appli...

It’s an early product and I’d really love any and all feedback I can get. If you or your team regularly use coding agents, please try it on an active project and see if it helps your agents learn and improve over time. It’s free for solo use.

records.title: Show HN: Rhubarb – build, edit, publish custom JavaScript/D3 data visualizations
records.author: adam_dataviz
records.storyText:
Last July, I was beginning to consider branching out on my own to take on data analytics work as a consultant.

As I experimented with AI, I realized how incredible it was at building custom data visualizations. The problem was that the AI outputs couldn't really live anywhere without having to manage all of the infrastructure yourself.

The generated code is only one piece of delivering an interactive visualization. You still need somewhere for the data to live, a way to keep the data fresh, hosting, access control, and version control for the code.

I started building Rhubarb as the platform that I wanted to use to deliver analytical products. Having been forced into using legacy point and click data visualization tools for years, I wanted to build the platform that would let me build the kinds of visualizations I wanted to build.

Over the last year the models improved so dramatically, that between that and my development background, Rhubarb turned into a real project.

My intent was to build an environment around AI’s ability to write code for visualizations, so that you could get from data and a concept to a published visualization all in one workflow.

The Rhubarb Assistant writes the code for your data transformations and data visualizations and lets you inspect the code to verify and validate what it produces. The environment pulls all of that together so that at the end of each request, there is a live version of the change rather than just a block of generated code.

For me, this has made it dramatically easier to build and publish interesting analytical visualizations while maintaining control over the analytical pipeline.

This has also produced some results I wasn’t really planning to build. Having been so impressed by it's ability to build any type of custom visualization I'd asked for so far, I asked for something a little absurd to test the boundaries. I asked the assistant to make something inspired by Monet’s water lilies, then I asked it to add frogs and to make them jump when you startled them.

In a couple of prompts I had created the silly interactive frog visualization that's in the demo, entirely from my phone. It is only a couple of prompts away from being a playable game, maybe you can get it there.

The public demo is deliberately limited. You can use the Rhubarb Assistant to modify live visualizations, inspect what it produces, and try building something from scratch. The full thing handles much more of the life cycle from connecting to data, managing and transforming it, to publishing your results.

Give it a try, I would like to hear what you think.

Try it: https://rhubarbviz.com/try?launch=1

View examples: https://rhubarbviz.com/demo-visualization-gallery

records.title: Show HN: Anxiety Checklist – 3 years of itterate with no success yet
records.author: seobuddy
records.storyText:
I lived with Anxiety Disorders (and Panic Attack, avoidance behavior) from 27 to 37 years old, at first I saw my general practionner who refer me to psychiatrist who listen to me 15 minutes and prescribe me anxiety pills

Where I come from (France), official data show 13% of population takes pills for anxiety, and I didn't want for personal reason increase that statistic.

Unfortunately, at that time (now I'm 44), all informations on the topic was very fragmented, and ultimately the self discovery journey to understand my trigger, find peace, and take control of my anxiety took way too much time.

For me Anxiety and avoidance behavior result in staying way too long in situation I should have avoided (relationship, business)

But in this journey, I also meet incredible therapist, daily relaxation method, and technique for self discovery that I accept it as part of a cool life journey.

4 years ago I decided I want to share this, first with a book (that I sold to 45 people ) and a Checklist (yes... not the right format, I was just replicating my other business "SEO Checklist") while building my content Hub, the Anxiety University, that grew from 0 to 78 human made article

Then I decided to invest into my own CBT Training Program and first hypnotherapy session but lost all money because the therapists I hired got cancer (and the other one hide the situation to burn my 30k invest to produce it)

I then pivot to a full fledge mobile app, without AI (more on that later) and cut a deal with a Neuro Psychologist in NY and Panic Expert in Australia to license their course. But the bundle inside the app looked too much as a "Upsell Money Grab" so I eventually shut this down recently.

3 Years later, Anxiety Checklist is DR70 and thanks to AI and Claude Code, I finally have a good app with proper tracking and can use data to improve my onboarding, understand better my audience, and itterate 10x faster (and cheaper) but with strong old school human made fondation.

Today I'm launching on Product Hunt with new onboarding showing 7% download to free trial conversion rate, and hope that I'll finally have something I can scale with ads.

For me it's not just about the money, I really like this mission, but as any business, I need the economic to make sense to add more content, hire more talent, and marketing to get more exposure.

Anyhow, the journey was fun, even though I burned 225k USD in this venture over 3 years... I called it my money pitt :))

My plan if paid aquisition fail is to put everything free and launch a therapist directory (the app is in complement of therapy, not a replacement)

3 Years, multiple pivot, still not profitable, that's my lame story, but still not giving up.

records.title: Show HN: Kursal, a decentralized E2E encrypted messenger
records.author: Kodeur_Kubik
records.storyText:
I'm building Kursal for over a year now. All backend is built in Rust for speed and safety.

No central server and no accounts. Peers connect over libp2p [1] and messages go through a Double Ratchet + PQXDH (Signal's protocol), so it's resistant to quantum attacks too.

I experimented with decentralization and encryption, and described it all on a technical paper [2]

All open source, of course, and I'd love having feedback!

[1] https://libp2p.io [2] https://kursal.chat/kursal.pdf

records.title: Show HN: Chow, a FOSS food diary
records.author: sltr
records.storyText:
Hi HN.

Today I'm showing off Chow.fit, a plain-text FOSS food diary written in Gleam. You can self-host it with the Dockerfile or just use the one I host on chow.fit.

Why does the world need another food diary app? Well, I can't speak for the whole world, but as for me:

I used MyFitnessPal back in 2017-2019. It was mostly tolerable with an ad blocker. A month ago due to numbers I didn't like, I wanted to start tracking calories again. I quickly noticed that in the MFP android app, the barcode scanner is now a paid feature. It felt like paying to use my own phone camera. Their web app is slow and stuck in 2013, so I made my own web app which better aligns with my values and goals. I've lost 5% of my body weight!

I like to call an app like this "un-SaaS" because it subverts a lot of the usual SaaS playbook.

- Distraction-free. No AI, no ads, no tracking, no engagement-hancing e.g. no activity/news feed. It logs food and gets out of the way.

- All features except sync work without a subscription.

- An optional subscription enables sync. A year covers my hosting costs and buys me a T-shirt.

- Sync is local-first. You can still log food e.g. in an airplane. The app syncs up when you go back online.

- If you stop the subscription, the app keeps working without sync.

- Your data is plain text files on your device. When SparkPeople shut down in 2021, its users could only download their daily totals. They lost everything else. That can't happen with Chow.

- It uses public food data (FDC and OFF), not proprietary

- It can import from MyFitnessPal using a bookmarklet to get your auth token which stays local.

- It has a desktop app, Android/iOS app, and a CLI. None currently shipped, but you can build from source.

Folks who track what they eat: Let me know what else you'd like to see!

records.title: Show HN: Dialedin.bio – Upload lab PDFs, log how you feel, see what lines up
records.author: redigaffi
records.storyText:
Hey Hackers!

I built the following app after some health issues I had. In short the app allows you to upload your bloodwork, and have all of your bloodwork in one place and not scattered around. You can create charts, see trends and patterns, fill in questionnaires on how you feel which you can add on the chart, together with trend lines, to easily find out what makes you healthier, and more "optimal".

You can checkout the app here https://dialedin.bio/

Also, if you are curious of one of my stacks, I was taking some supplements, and my testosterone has risen a bit, together with my mood and libido, you can see my experimente here

- https://dialedin.bio/c/cZIUe6rzO__KIQ193oUZvg

Free while on beta!

records.title: Show HN: Gatling.chat – The Turbo Messenger for LinkedIn
records.author: mlukaszczyk
records.storyText:
Everyone who does a lot of prospecting, networking and sales on Linkedin just knows how painful the native Linkedin messenger is. For another business, I am generating around 100-200 lead-connections per week. Without this product it's really insufferable. So I built this.

Gatling.chat is the Turbo Messenger for Linkedin. Inbox-Zero principles. Split inboxes, follow-ups and sequences, snippets, cleared from the keyboard in a beautiful and snappy desktop app. Built to keep your account within LinkedIn’s rules on automation.
